claims.text: Group A strep in children: rapid antigen test in the office; if negative, send a throat culture.
claims.quote: one strategy in children is to do a rapid strep screen (rapid antigen detection test) in the office and treat empirically if positive, and if negative, send a formal culture to a laboratory for testing.

claims.text: Point-of-care NAAT (PCR) returns in about 15 to 30 minutes and is more sensitive than rapid antigen tests.
claims.quote: Point-of-care NAATs (eg, polymerase chain reaction) can provide results in approximately 15 to 30 minutes to rapidly inform clinical decision-making; they offer improved sensitivity compared to rapid antigen-detection tests while maintaining specificity

claims.text: Mono, gonorrhea or HIV testing only when clinically suspected.
claims.quote: Testing for mononucleosis, gonorrhea, or HIV infection is done only when clinically suspected.

claims.text: Abscess of unclear location or extent: immediate CT of the neck.
claims.quote: Many abscesses are managed clinically, but if location and extent are unclear, immediate CT of the neck should be done.

claims.text: Possible epiglottitis: examine a child's pharynx only in the operating room.
claims.quote: If epiglottitis is considered, directly examine a child's pharynx only in the operating room to minimize the risk of complete airway obstruction.

claims.text: Lateral neck X-ray only for a child who is not seriously ill and has no respiratory symptoms.
claims.quote: Patients who do not appear seriously ill and have no respiratory symptoms may have lateral neck radiographs to look for edematous epiglottis.
